subject: Reasoning
topic: Statement and Assumptions — Critical Reasoning (W12 B1)

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Use staircase instead of lift for better health.' — Appeared on a hospital notice board.
Assumptions:
I. People generally prefer lifts over stairs.
II. Staircase use improves health.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: C is correct. For the advice to be meaningful: I must be true — if people already used stairs, the advice would be unnecessary (implicit: people prefer lifts). II must be true — the advice explicitly claims a health benefit (implicit: stairs are better for health). An assumption is something that must be taken as true for the statement to make sense. Both are implicit in this notice. Trap: 'Only II' ignores that the notice is persuasive (implying current behaviour is lift-use); 'Only I' ignores the factual health claim.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Wanted: Experienced accountant for a reputed firm. Apply within 7 days.'
Assumptions:
I. The firm has a vacancy for an accountant.
II. Qualified accountants will respond to this advertisement.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: C is correct. I is implicit — you only advertise if there is an actual vacancy. II is implicit — the advertisement is placed with the expectation that suitable applicants will read and respond to it; otherwise there is no point advertising. Both assumptions underlie the action of placing the advertisement. Trap: 'Only I' ignores the purpose (II); 'Only II' ignores the basic reason for the ad (I).

questions.stem:
Statement: 'If you drive after drinking, you could kill someone.'
Assumptions:
I. Drunk driving increases the likelihood of accidents.
II. People sometimes drive after drinking.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: C is correct. I is implicit — the warning presupposes that drunk driving is dangerous (higher accident risk). If drinking didn't affect driving, the warning would be baseless. II is implicit — the warning is directed at people who might drive after drinking, implying this behaviour actually occurs. A warning that addressed impossible behaviour would be pointless. Both assumptions must be true for the statement to have purpose. Trap: 'Only I' is too narrow — the warning also needs a real-world audience (II).

questions.stem:
Statement: 'The government has decided to build a new metro line connecting the airport to the city centre.'
Assumptions:
I. There is significant traffic congestion between the airport and the city.
II. People travel between the airport and the city centre regularly.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: C is correct. I is implicit — the government invests in metro infrastructure to solve a transport problem; congestion or capacity demand is a common reason. II is definitely implicit — you don't build transport infrastructure for a route nobody uses. Regular travel demand must be assumed. Both underlie the government decision. Trap: Some might dispute I arguing the metro might be for speed rather than congestion, but the general transport problem (I in its broad sense) is still assumed.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Do not use mobile phones while driving — It is dangerous and illegal.'
Assumptions:
I. People use mobile phones while driving.
II. Mobile phone use impairs driving ability.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: C is correct. I is implicit — warnings against a behaviour assume that the behaviour occurs (otherwise why warn?). II is implicit — the word 'dangerous' directly reflects the assumption that mobile use impairs driving. Both are foundational to the statement. This is a classic two-assumption SSC question where both are clearly embedded.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Train X arriving at Platform 3 is delayed by 45 minutes.' — Public address announcement.
Assumptions:
I. Passengers are at the station waiting for Train X.
II. Trains sometimes get delayed.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: A is correct. I is implicit — the announcement is made specifically so that waiting passengers are informed; without an audience of waiting passengers, the announcement would be pointless. II is NOT a valid assumption implicit in THIS statement — the statement is a specific factual report (Train X is delayed); the general truth that 'trains sometimes get delayed' is widely known general knowledge, not an unstated assumption that the speaker relies on. An assumption must be something specifically assumed for THIS particular statement to be rational — I qualifies, II does not. Trap: 'Both' — II seems logical but is a known fact, not an assumed unstated premise.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'We must plant more trees to reduce air pollution in our cities.'
Assumptions:
I. Air pollution in cities is currently at unacceptable levels.
II. Trees help reduce air pollution.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: C is correct. I is implicit — the recommendation to 'reduce air pollution' implies that current pollution levels are a problem (otherwise there's nothing to reduce). II is implicit — the proposal to plant trees as a pollution solution assumes trees effectively reduce air pollution. Both underlie the recommendation. Trap: 'Only II' ignores I; but I is also implicit because the call to act implies the problem exists at a significant level.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'The best way to pass the SSC exam is to practise previous year question papers.'
Assumptions:
I. The SSC exam follows a consistent pattern across years.
II. Other study methods are completely ineffective.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: A is correct. I is implicit — you can only benefit from previous year papers if the exam pattern remains reasonably consistent; if every exam were completely different, past papers would be useless. I must be assumed. II is NOT implicit — the statement says PYQs are the 'best way', not the 'only way'. The word 'best' does not imply all other methods are completely ineffective; it only implies PYQs are MORE effective. II overstates what the statement implies. Only I is implicit.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Students who fail to submit assignments on time will not be allowed to sit for the exam.'
Assumptions:
I. Some students may not submit assignments on time.
II. Exams are an important part of the evaluation process.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: A is correct. I is implicit — the rule is created in anticipation that the behaviour (late submission) may occur; a rule against something assumes that thing is possible. I must be true for the rule to have a purpose. II is NOT implicit — the statement uses 'not allowed to sit for the exam' as a penalty, but doesn't presuppose that exams are important; the statement is about the rule of compliance, not the importance of exams. The threat of exam exclusion works as a deterrent regardless of whether exams are 'important'. Only I is implicit.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'The school has decided to introduce yoga in the morning assembly for all students.'
Assumptions:
I. Yoga improves physical and mental well-being.
II. All students are currently unhealthy.

options.option_text: Both I and II are implicit

questions.explanation: A is correct. I is implicit — the school introduces yoga expecting it to be beneficial; this presupposes yoga has health benefits (well-being improvement). I must be assumed. II is NOT implicit — the school can introduce yoga as a general well-being practice even for healthy students; yoga is not only for the unhealthy. The statement does not imply students are currently unwell. II is too extreme and not necessary for the decision to be rational. Only I is implicit.
